feedback.problem: Given the function $f(x)=(x-1)^{3}{e}^{x}$ for $x\in [0,\infty ),$ which of the following statements are true?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(x-1)^{3}{e}^{x}+3(x-1)^{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}{e}^{x}(x-1+3) \\  & =(x-1)^{2}(x+2){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
(x-1)^{2}(x+2){e}^{x}=0\,⟹\,x=-2,\,x=1.
$$

Note that we used the fact that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all values of $x.$

So, $x=1$ is the only stationary point of $f(x)$ on $[0,\infty ).$ Next, to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=0,2$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =(0-1)^{2}(0+2){e}^{0}=2>0 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =(2-1)^{2}(2+2){e}^{2}=4{e}^{2}>0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $[0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $0$ |  | $2$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ |  | $↗$ |

The first derivative does not change sign at $x=1.$ Therefore, we conclude that $x=1$ is neither a minimum nor a maximum.

Therefore, the first derivative test shows that the function has no local extrema on $[0,\infty ).$
